Styles / 04 / Pilot

Memphis

The postmodern style of the Memphis Group, founded in Milan by Ettore Sottsass and active from 1980 to 1987: bright clashing colors, printed laminates, squiggles and speckles, and furniture built from bold, toy-like forms.

Playful / Loud / Irreverent / Postmodern

Visual grammar

  • Clashing brights. Pink, yellow, turquoise, red, and black together, often at full saturation.
  • Printed pattern. Laminate patterns such as squiggles, speckles, and bacteria-like marks cover whole surfaces.
  • Toy geometry. Cylinders, spheres, arches, zigzags, and stepped forms combine like building blocks.
  • Deliberate imbalance. Parts meet at odd angles and different scales. Symmetry is avoided.
  • Black-and-white grids. Grid patterns in black and white act as a neutral foil for strong colors.

What connects the references

Furniture defines the style: Sottsass’s Carlton and Casablanca, Shire’s Bel Air chair, and De Lucchi’s First chair combine laminate color with toy-like parts.

Pattern is equally central. Du Pasquier’s Gabon textile and the 1985 swatch card show the prints that covered surfaces.

Christoph Radl’s logotype and leaflet show how the group presented itself in print: blocky letters, black grounds, and labelled pattern samples.

Most Memphis references are link-only, because the works are in copyright. The exception is a screenshot of Abet Laminati’s Bacterio page, which shows the laminate pattern still in production. The Memphis Milano company website was captured but not kept: it sells the work but is not itself in the style.

Lineage

  • Reaction against Modernist good design. Memphis rejected the functional restraint associated with the Bauhaus and later modernism.
  • Influenced by Studio Alchimia. Sottsass worked with Studio Alchimia, a Milan avant-garde group founded in 1976, before he founded Memphis.
  • Influenced by Pop art. Bright commercial color and references to popular culture.
  • Related to Corporate Memphis. A 2010s flat illustration style named after the group. It shares bright color but not the group’s patterns or furniture forms.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Four or more saturated colors appear together, including pinks and turquoises.
  • Repeating patterns such as squiggles, dots, speckles, or grids fill surfaces.
  • Forms are geometric but playful, with odd combinations of scale and angle.

Rules it out

  • A restrained palette of one or two colors.
  • Strict grid alignment and quiet typography carry the design.
  • Photographic realism or glossy 3D rendering dominates.

Often confused with

Corporate Memphis
Corporate Memphis is flat vector illustration of people with long limbs. Memphis is about pattern, color, and object form.
Bauhaus
Bauhaus shapes are elementary and the palette is primary. Memphis is irregular, decorative, and uses many non-primary colors.
Neo-brutalism
Neo-brutalism also uses bright colors, but relies on thick outlines and hard shadows, not pattern.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Combine at least four saturated colors, for example pink, yellow, turquoise, and black.
  • Fill backgrounds or panels with a pattern: squiggles, confetti dots, or a black-and-white grid.
  • Place geometric shapes such as circles, half circles, triangles, and zigzags around content, at odd angles.
  • Use a bold display face for headings and keep body text plain for reading.

Keep the function

  • Do not put body text on top of a busy pattern. Use a solid panel under text.
  • Do not use gradients or realistic shadows.
  • Do not reduce the style to cartoon people. That is Corporate Memphis, a different style.

Useful directions: festivals, youth brands, galleries, playful product launches.
